one_liner: Header-only C++20 concurrent garbage collector whose allocation path beats malloc-backed unique_ptr/shared_ptr for small objects on macOS.
what_it_does: SGCL is a header-only C++20 tracing garbage collector, now grown into a 15-module application platform (async, net, crypto, codec and more) built on managed pointers. You allocate with make_tracked<T>() and hold objects in sgcl::tracked_ptr (collected when unreachable, cycles included), sgcl::unique_ptr (deterministic destruction) or root_ptr (for globals and std containers). It is not a drop-in replacement for malloc or std smart pointers: code has to adopt the sgcl pointer and container types and follow its placement rules.
how_it_is_fast: Allocation is a bitmap pop from a per-thread page allocator plus one byte of state, with no lock or barrier, and freeing moves off the mutator onto a collector thread that sweeps and runs destructors. The collector is a concurrent, non-moving, generational (sticky mark bits plus card marking) mark-and-sweep with a Dijkstra insertion barrier, no stop-the-world phase and no safepoints; stacks are scanned conservatively while threads run, and the heap is traced through per-type pointer maps narrowed by elimination. Marking is parallelised over helper threads with page-order tracing and a prefetch window.
when_to_use: Pointer-heavy C++ code with shared or cyclic graphs (lock-free structures, ASTs, actor/channel programs) where shared_ptr reference counting and destructor cascades cost too much: shared_ptr drop-all took 68-171 ms vs microseconds for SGCL on the shared-graph benchmark.
Allocation-heavy workloads of small objects (32 B) on 1-24 threads where wall time on the mutator matters more than total CPU.
Programs that copy pointers to shared objects across threads: 1.4-1.9 ns per copy vs 125-149 ns for contended shared_ptr.
Projects that want Go-style concurrency (tasks, channels) inside C++ without a separate reclamation scheme such as hazard pointers or epochs.
Apple Silicon macOS builds with Apple clang, the only tested platform.
when_not_to_use: Linux, Windows or x86-64 targets in production: the current version is built and tested on Apple Silicon only, and no number has been reproduced elsewhere.
Memory-constrained programs: binary-trees depth 21 peaks at 292 MB vs 134 MB for unique_ptr, and garbage waits for a cycle.
Many threads allocating 256 B objects: 71.4 ns vs 23.5 ns for unique_ptr on 24 threads.

CPU-budgeted or core-saturated systems: the win moves destruction to collector threads, so process CPU time is much closer to the baseline than wall time (9.41 vs 12.39 s at binary-trees depth 21) and collector threads compete with mutators for cores.
Code that needs destructors to run promptly on tracked objects, uses raw pointers as owning references, or stores pointers in std containers, unions, std::variant or std::function.

integration.dependencies: none for the library (CMake interface target optional); on Apple systems the target links Security, CoreFoundation and, for HEIF, ImageIO/CoreGraphics/Accelerate; tests need googletest, zlib, libbz2 and OpenSSL 3
integration.min_toolchain: C++20; tested only with Apple clang (21.0 in the published benchmarks); gcc on Windows discouraged
integration.platforms: macOS on Apple Silicon tested; Linux, Windows and x86-64 written for but pending
integration.thread_safety: Concurrent collector; any thread can allocate and copy pointers, threads are registered on first pointer copy; atomic<tracked_ptr> with compare-exchange provided for shared mutable slots
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — make_tracked returns an sgcl::unique_ptr with familiar semantics, but objects must be allocated through SGCL and held in sgcl pointer and container types; it does not replace malloc or std::shared_ptr transparently

gotchas: A tracked_ptr may live only on a thread's own stack or inside a managed object; in a global, a std container, heap memory from new, a heap-copied lambda or a plain coroutine frame it is never scanned and its object can be collected (use root_ptr there). Alternate signal stacks, fibers and ucontext stacks are not scanned.

A tracked_ptr must never share storage with data (union with a value, std::variant, std::any, std::function inline storage) because per-type pointer maps are narrowed by elimination; use sgcl::variant, any, function and expected instead.
Destructors of tracked objects run on collector threads in no particular order; a destructor may not touch its tracked_ptr members except through if_alive().

The headline baseline is macOS libmalloc's nano zone; earlier runs with MallocNanoZone=0 made the unique_ptr/shared_ptr columns about a quarter slower, and the Go/Java columns come from an older -O2 run.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The siblings (mimalloc-class allocators such as Kaname-Shiki or FastAlloc, pool allocators such as fast-alloc, mem++) speed up malloc/free behind the same manual or reference-counted ownership; pick SGCL when the cost you want gone is shared_ptr reference counting, destructor cascades or a reclamation scheme for shared and cyclic graphs, and you can adopt a GC pointer type. If you only need faster malloc on Linux, a sibling allocator is the safer choice.
verified_claims_summary: On a Mac Studio (Apple M2 Ultra, macOS 26.5, Apple clang 21.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG, libc++, macOS nano-zone malloc), the repo's own benchmarks/ programs show a 32 B allocation at 2.8 ns on one thread vs 17.1 ns for std::unique_ptr and 16.3 ns for std::shared_ptr (about 6x), narrowing to 11.7 vs 23.2 ns on 24 threads, while 256 B on 24 threads is about 3x slower than unique_ptr (71.4 vs 23.5 ns). Binary-trees depth 21 runs in 4.43 s wall vs 12.42 s for unique_ptr, but with 9.41 vs 12.39 s process CPU and 292 vs 134 MB peak memory.
status_note: Very actively developed (last commit 2026-10-05) by a single author, Apache-2.0 and header-only so it is easy to vendor, but the API is pre-1.0 with stability promised only from 1.0.0, and only macOS on Apple Silicon is tested.
